LABOUR'S BANK CARD BALLOT BOX

NO PHOTO. NO FACE CHECK. JUST A NAME ON A CARD.

By Steve English   |   11 October 2026

Labour wants to change Britain's voter identification rules so that an ordinary qualifying bank card can be used to vote at a polling station.

Not a photographic driving licence. Not a passport. A qualifying UK-issued bank card bearing the registered elector's name.

And Britain's independent Electoral Commission has warned that introducing bank cards as voter ID will weaken security. [2]

Under the Representation of the People Bill, UK-issued bank cards would become an accepted form of identification in Great Britain. The Government says this would help eligible voters who lack currently accepted identification. [1]

BUT HERE'S THE QUESTION THE GOVERNMENT NEEDS TO ANSWER.

How does a polling station official know that the person holding the bank card is actually its owner?

A bank card generally has no photograph. Another person's card can be borrowed or stolen. A matching name on a card does not, by itself, establish a matching identity.

EVEN THE ELECTORAL WATCHDOG IS WARNING THEM

“Introducing bank cards as voter ID will weaken security.”

That is the Electoral Commission's own assessment, published in its briefing on the Bill. It explains that bank cards do not have photographs and may not display full names, making it harder for polling staff to verify identity. Unlike passports or driving licences, bank cards lack a common format and standard visual validation features. [2] [3]

Yet the Government is continuing to pursue the change.

WHY PHOTOGRAPHIC ID MATTERS

The purpose of photographic voter identification is straightforward: it helps establish that the person standing at the polling station is the person entitled to cast that particular vote.

That matters when considering potential electoral abuse. A person who is not legally entitled to vote could attempt to impersonate a registered elector. So could an otherwise eligible voter attempting to vote in someone else's name.

Someone could also attempt to vote more than once by impersonating different registered electors. Such conduct is illegal; accepting bank cards would not legalise it or remove electoral-register checks. But the absence of a photograph would remove one means of detecting an impostor.

THE COMMON WEAKNESS? IMPERSONATION.

Photographic ID enables staff to compare the person with the picture. A bank card cannot perform that function.

Existing rules also accommodate people whose faces are covered for religious reasons: identity can be checked privately, including by female staff where available. With a non-photographic bank card, however, there is no photograph to compare, regardless of whether the voter's face is covered.

None of these scenarios proves that illegal migrants, religious communities or other groups are committing widespread voting fraud. The relevant question is whether the proposed rules could make personation harder to detect.

Registration checks whether a named elector is entitled to vote. Photographic ID helps check whether the person presenting that name is the right person. Those are distinct safeguards.

WHAT PROBLEM IS LABOUR TRYING TO SOLVE?

The Government argues that the existing identification rules are too restrictive and that accepting bank cards would reduce the proportion of people without an accepted form of ID from an estimated 2–4% to below 1%. [1]

Electoral Commission research found that fewer than 0.1% of people who tried to vote in person at the 2024 general election were ultimately unable to vote because they lacked accepted ID. It also found that around 4% of non-voters said the ID requirement was a factor in not voting. Both findings deserve attention. [3]

There is a genuine debate about accessibility. But free photographic Voter Authority Certificates already exist for eligible voters without accepted photo ID. Why not make those easier to obtain rather than introducing a form of identification without a photograph?

LABOUR WAS WARNED MONTHS AGO

The security concern is not a new October discovery. The Electoral Commission raised its objections in parliamentary briefings earlier this year. The Bill was introduced in February, considered in Commons committee in March and April, and proceeded through further Commons stages in September. [2] [5]

It would be misleading to say the proposal was secret or that scrutiny was entirely bypassed. But the fact remains: the Government has continued with the bank-card provision despite the independent watchdog's documented concerns.

THIS IS ABOUT THE INTEGRITY OF THE BALLOT

Voter identification exists in part to deter personation — someone voting in another person's name.

Accepting bank cards does not abolish voter registration, eligibility requirements or the criminal offence of personation. But it removes the photographic comparison for anyone using that form of ID.

A BANK CARD PROVES THAT SOMEONE HAS A BANK CARD. IT DOES NOT PROVE WHO IS HOLDING IT.

If ministers believe the alternative checks are adequate, they should explain precisely how polling station staff are expected to distinguish a legitimate elector from someone presenting another person's card.

The Electoral Commission has raised the security question. The Government should answer it directly before the rules change.

Potential security vulnerabilities are not evidence that a particular person or group has committed electoral fraud. The Bill's provisions discussed here are proposals, not a statement that the changes are already in force.
